questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Obtain an expression for the fringe width in the interference of light of wavelength λ from a double slit of slit separation d. The screen is at distance D from the slits.
questions.solution: The path difference at a point P on the screen at distance y from the centre is Δ = d sinθ ≈ dy/D. For constructive interference Δ = mλ, so y_m = mλD/d. The fringe width is the separation of consecutive maxima: β = y_(m+1) - y_m = λD/d. Bright and dark fringes are equally spaced when θ is small.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Obtain an expression for the radius of the m-th order bright ring in the case of Newton's rings.
questions.solution: For a plano-convex lens of radius R on a flat plate, the thickness of the air film at radius r is t ≈ r²/(2R). In reflected light, bright rings satisfy 2t = (m - 1/2)λ for m = 1, 2, 3, ... Substituting t gives r_m² = (m - 1/2)λR, so r_m = sqrt((2m - 1)λR/2). The diameter is D_m = sqrt(2(2m - 1)λR).

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Explain the interference pattern in the case of a wedge-shaped thin film.
questions.solution: A wedge-shaped air film has a thickness that increases linearly along the wedge. For reflected light, the condition 2t = (m + 1/2)λ gives straight, parallel bright fringes, with dark fringes midway between them. The fringe spacing is β = λ/(2α), where α is the wedge angle, so the fringes are equally spaced and become closer as the wedge angle increases.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: A soap film (n = 1.33) in air is 482 nm thick. It is illuminated with white light at normal incidence. Which wavelengths will reinforce in reflected light? Which will reinforce in transmitted light?
questions.solution: For reflection from a film in air there is a phase reversal at the top surface only. Constructive reflection: 2nt = (m + 1/2)λ, so λ = 4nt/(2m + 1) = 4 × 1.33 × 482/(2m + 1) = 2564/(2m + 1) nm. Values: 2564 nm (m = 0, IR), 855 nm (m = 1), 513 nm (m = 2, green), 366 nm (m = 3, UV). The visible reflected wavelength is therefore about 513 nm. For transmitted light the conditions are interchanged: 2nt = mλ, so λ = 1282/m nm, giving 1282 nm (m = 1), 641 nm (m = 2, red) and 427 nm (m = 3, violet). Thus visible transmitted light is reinforced near 641 nm and 427 nm.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: How many complete fringes appear between the first minima of the fringe envelope on either side of the central maximum for a double-slit pattern if λ = 557 nm, slit separation d = 0.150 mm and slit width a = 0.030 mm? What is the ratio of the intensity of the third fringe to the side of the centre to that of the central fringe?
questions.solution: The envelope minima occur when a sinθ = λ. Interference maxima occur when d sinθ = mλ. A maximum is missing when d/a = m, so here d/a = 5 and the fifth-order fringe is missing. Between the first envelope minima on either side the visible orders are m = -4 to +4, giving 2 × 4 + 1 = 9 complete fringes. For the third fringe, the intensity is I = I0 (sinβ/β)² cos²α with a/d = 0.2. At m = 3, β = πa sinθ/λ = 3πa/d = 0.6π, so sinβ/β = sin(0.6π)/(0.6π) = 0.951/1.885 = 0.505. The ratio is therefore 0.505² ≈ 0.25, i.e. about 25% of the central intensity.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: The diameter of the tenth bright ring in a Newton's rings apparatus changes from 1.42 cm to 1.27 cm when a liquid is introduced between the lens and the plate. Find the refractive index of the liquid.
questions.solution: For the same ring, D² ∝ λ/n, so D_air/D_liquid = sqrt(n). Hence n = (D_air/D_liquid)² = (1.42/1.27)² ≈ 1.25.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Explain Michelson's interferometer and how it is used to determine the wavelength of monochromatic light.
questions.solution: A beam from the source is split by a partially silvered plate into two perpendicular paths, reflected by two mirrors and recombined. The path difference produces circular interference fringes. Moving one mirror by a distance d changes the path difference by 2d. If N fringes cross the field of view, 2d = Nλ, so λ = 2d/N. Counting fringes for a measured mirror displacement therefore gives the wavelength.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: A Newton's rings set-up in air is used to determine the radius of curvature of a lens. The radii of the n-th and (n + 20)-th bright rings are 0.162 cm and 0.368 cm in light of wavelength 546 nm. Calculate the radius of curvature of the lower surface of the lens.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: A thin film of acetone (n = 1.25) coats a thick glass plate (n = 1.50). Plane light waves of variable wavelength are incident normally. On viewing the reflected wave, complete destructive interference occurs at 600 nm and constructive interference at 700 nm. Calculate the minimum thickness of the acetone film.
questions.solution: Both the air-acetone and acetone-glass interfaces involve reflection from a denser medium, so the two reflected waves have no net phase difference. Destructive reflection requires 2nt = (m + 1/2)λ and constructive reflection requires 2nt = pλ. Using 600 nm destructive and 700 nm constructive: (m + 1/2)600 = p700. The smallest solution is m = 3, p = 3, giving 2nt = 2100 nm. Hence t = 2100/(2 × 1.25) = 840 nm.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: White light reflected at perpendicular incidence from a soap film (n = 1.33) in air has, in the visible spectrum, an interference maximum at 600 nm and a minimum at 450 nm with no minimum in between. What is the film thickness, assumed uniform?
questions.solution: With one phase reversal (air-film), constructive reflection is 2nt = (m + 1/2)λ and destructive reflection is 2nt = pλ. Using the 600 nm maximum and the next 450 nm minimum: (m + 1/2)600 = p450. The lowest consistent integers are m = 1 and p = 2, so 2nt = 900 nm and t = 900/(2 × 1.33) ≈ 338 nm. No other minimum lies between 450 nm and 600 nm, as required.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Design a double-slit system (find the slit separation in terms of the slit width) in which the fourth fringe, not counting the central maximum, is missing.
questions.solution: The m-th interference maximum coincides with the first diffraction minimum when d sinθ = mλ and a sinθ = λ, i.e. d/a = m. For the fourth fringe to be missing, d/a = 4, so the slit separation must be four times the slit width: d = 4a.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: In a double-slit experiment the screen is 52 cm from the slits, the wavelength is 480 nm, the slit separation is 0.12 mm and the slit width is 0.025 mm. What is the spacing between adjacent fringes? What is the distance from the central maximum to the first minimum of the fringe envelope?

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Obtain an expression for the intensity in a double-slit interference pattern using a phasor diagram.
questions.solution: Let the two coherent waves have equal amplitude a and phase difference δ = (2π/λ)d sinθ. In the phasor diagram the resultant of two equal phasors with angle δ between them has amplitude A = 2a cos(δ/2). Since intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, I = I0 cos²(δ/2) = I0 cos²(πd sinθ/λ), where I0 is the intensity of each wave. Maxima occur when δ = 2mπ (d sinθ = mλ) and minima when δ = (2m + 1)π.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Obtain an expression for the width of a principal maximum at an angle θ in the diffraction pattern due to multiple slits.
questions.solution: For N slits of spacing d, the intensity is I = I0 (sinNδ/2 / sinδ/2)² with δ = 2πd sinθ/λ. Principal maxima occur when δ = 2mπ. The first zero on either side occurs when Nδ/2 changes by π, i.e. Δδ = 2π/N. Since dδ = (2πd cosθ/λ)dθ, the angular half-width is Δθ = λ/(Nd cosθ) and the full width is 2λ/(Nd cosθ). Thus the maximum becomes narrower as N increases.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Monochromatic light of wavelength 538 nm falls on a slit of width 25.2 μm. The screen is 3.48 m from the slit. Consider a point 1.13 cm from the central maximum. Calculate the ratio of the intensity at this point to the intensity at the central maximum.
questions.solution: For a single slit, I/I0 = (sinβ/β)² with β = πa sinθ/λ ≈ πay/(λD). Here β = π × 25.2×10^-6 × 0.0113/(538×10^-9 × 3.48) = 0.478 rad. Then sinβ/β = 0.460/0.478 = 0.962, so I/I0 = 0.962² ≈ 0.925.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Explain Rayleigh's criterion for resolving images due to a circular aperture.
questions.solution: A circular aperture produces an Airy pattern rather than a point image. Two point objects are just resolved when the central maximum of one diffraction pattern falls on the first minimum of the other. For a circular aperture this occurs at the angular separation θ = 1.22λ/D, where D is the aperture diameter. Smaller wavelengths and larger apertures therefore give better resolution.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: A converging lens of diameter 32 mm has focal length 24 cm. What angular separation must two distant point objects have to satisfy Rayleigh's criterion at a wavelength of 550 nm? How far apart are the centres of the diffraction patterns in the focal plane?

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: A source of light of two wavelengths (660 nm and 440 nm) is used in a diffraction experiment. The light is incident normally on a grating. Find the ratio of the angular widths of the zeroth-order principal maximum for 660 nm to that for 440 nm.
questions.solution: The angular width of a principal maximum is Δθ = 2λ/(Nd cosθ). At the zeroth order cosθ = 1, so Δθ ∝ λ. Therefore the ratio is 660/440 = 1.5.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: A grating has 40,000 rulings spread over 76 mm. (a) What is its expected dispersion for sodium light of wavelength 589 nm in the first order? (b) What is its resolving power in this order?

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: A grating has 10^4 slits with a slit separation of 2100 nm. It is illuminated with sodium light of wavelength 589 nm. Find the angular positions of all principal maxima observed.
questions.solution: The grating equation is d sinθ = mλ, so sinθ = 589m/2100 = 0.2805m. Since |sinθ| ≤ 1, m can be 0, ±1, ±2, ±3. The angles are: m = 0 at 0°; m = ±1 at sin⁻¹(0.2805) = 16.3°; m = ±2 at sin⁻¹(0.561) = 34.1°; m = ±3 at sin⁻¹(0.8415) = 57.3°. The fourth order would require sinθ > 1 and is not observed.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Given a grating with 400 rulings/mm, how many orders of the entire visible spectrum (400-700 nm) can be produced?
questions.solution: d = 1/400 mm = 2.5×10^-6 m. For an order to contain the entire visible spectrum, the longest wavelength must satisfy mλmax ≤ d. Thus m ≤ 2.5×10^-6/700×10^-9 = 3.57, so three complete orders (m = 1, 2, 3) can be produced on each side of the central maximum.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Deduce an expression for the focal length of a zone plate. Write the difference between a zone plate and a convex lens.
questions.solution: For the n-th Fresnel zone, the path difference between the edge and the centre is nλ/2. With zone radius r_n and focal length f, r_n² ≈ nλf, so f = r_n²/(nλ). A zone plate therefore has multiple foci at f, f/3, f/5, ... and its focal length depends on wavelength (strong chromatic aberration). Unlike a convex lens, it works by diffraction rather than refraction and can form a real image even for X-rays.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: A beam of green light is diffracted by a slit of width 0.550 mm. The diffraction pattern forms on a wall 2.06 m beyond the slit. The distance to the position of the first zero intensity from the central bright fringe is 2.05 mm. Calculate the wavelength of the laser light.
questions.solution: The first minimum of a single slit occurs at a sinθ = λ, and for small angles sinθ ≈ y/D. Hence λ = ay/D = 0.550×10^-3 × 2.05×10^-3/2.06 ≈ 5.47×10^-7 m = 547 nm.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: A single slit is illuminated by light of wavelengths λA and λB, chosen so that the first diffraction minimum of the λA component coincides with the second minimum of the λB component. What is the relationship between the two wavelengths? Do any other minima in the two patterns coincide?
questions.solution: For a single slit the minima satisfy a sinθ = nλ. Coincidence of the first minimum of A with the second minimum of B gives λA = 2λB. In general mλA = nλB becomes 2mλB = nλB, so n = 2m. Hence every minimum of A coincides with an even-order minimum of B, and the two patterns share every second minimum of B.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Explain optical activity with a diagram.
questions.solution: Certain materials (e.g. quartz, sugar solution) rotate the plane of polarization of plane-polarized light passing through them; they are optically active. The rotation φ is proportional to the path length l and concentration c: φ = [α] l c, where [α] is the specific rotation. The rotation is clockwise (dextrorotatory) for some substances and anticlockwise (laevorotatory) for others.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Explain the phenomenon of double refraction with a diagram indicating the directions of polarization for the two beams.
questions.solution: When unpolarized light enters an anisotropic crystal such as calcite, it splits into two refracted rays. The ordinary ray obeys Snell's law and is polarized perpendicular to the principal section; the extraordinary ray does not obey Snell's law and is polarized in the principal section. The two rays are therefore plane-polarized in mutually perpendicular directions and travel with different velocities.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: When red light in vacuum is incident at the polarizing angle on a certain glass slab, the angle of refraction is 31.8°. What are (i) the refractive index of the glass and (ii) the polarizing angle?
questions.solution: At the polarizing angle θp, the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular, so θp + r = 90°. Thus θp = 90° - 31.8° = 58.2°. By Brewster's law, n = tanθp = tan58.2° ≈ 1.61.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Explain the method of producing plane-polarized light by refraction in a stack of glass plates.
questions.solution: When unpolarized light strikes a glass plate at the Brewster angle, the reflected component is completely polarized in the plane of incidence. The transmitted light is partially polarized. In a stack of parallel plates, each plate removes more of the perpendicular component through reflection, so after passing through many plates the transmitted beam becomes almost completely plane-polarized in the plane of incidence.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Derive an expression for the thickness of a half-wave plate.
questions.solution: A wave plate introduces a phase difference between the ordinary and extraordinary rays: Δφ = (2π/λ)(n_o - n_e)t. For a half-wave plate the path difference must be λ/2, so (n_o - n_e)t = λ/2 and t = λ/[2(n_o - n_e)]. Such a plate rotates the plane of polarization of linearly polarized light by 90° for the appropriate orientation.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: A left circularly polarized beam (λ = 589 nm) is incident normally on a calcite crystal (optic axis parallel to the surface) of thickness 0.005141 mm. What is the state of polarization of the emergent beam? Given n_e = 1.48640 and n_o = 1.65835.
questions.solution: The path difference is (n_o - n_e)t = (1.65835 - 1.48640) × 5.141×10^-6 m = 8.841×10^-7 m. In wavelengths this is 8.841×10^-7/5.89×10^-7 = 1.50λ. A retardation of 1.5λ is equivalent to a half-wave plate (an odd multiple of λ/2), which reverses the handedness of circular polarization. The emergent beam is therefore right circularly polarized.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Explain a wave packet and its (i) group speed and (ii) phase speed.
questions.solution: A wave packet is a localized wave disturbance formed by superposing many plane waves of slightly different frequencies and wavelengths. The phase speed vp = ω/k is the speed of a single monochromatic component. The group speed vg = dω/dk is the speed of the envelope (and of the particle). They are related by vg = vp + k dvp/dk = vp - λ dvp/dλ; in a non-dispersive medium the two are equal.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Sketch the lowest three energy states, wave functions and probability densities for a particle in a one-dimensional infinite potential well.
questions.solution: For a well from 0 to L, ψ_n = sqrt(2/L) sin(nπx/L) and E_n = n²h²/(8mL²). n = 1: a single half-sine hump, with |ψ|² maximum at the centre and nodes at the walls. n = 2: two humps with a node at L/2. n = 3: three humps with nodes at L/3 and 2L/3. The number of nodes inside the well is n - 1, and the energy spacing increases with n.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Sketch the wave functions and probability densities for the lowest three energy states of a particle in a potential well of finite height.
questions.solution: Inside the well the wave functions are sinusoidal; outside they decay exponentially as e^(-α|x|) because E < U0. Unlike the infinite well, ψ does not vanish at the walls, so the wave function leaks into the classically forbidden region. For the ground state there is no internal node; the first excited state has one node, and the second has two. The probability density extends slightly beyond the well edges, which allows tunnelling.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: An alpha particle in a nucleus can be modelled as a particle in a box of length 1.0 × 10^-14 m. Estimate the wavelength, momentum and energy of the alpha particle in its first excited state (n = 2).

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: The lifetime of an electron in the state n = 2 in hydrogen is 10 ns. What is the uncertainty in the electron energy in this state? Also estimate the resulting line width.
questions.solution: ΔE Δt ≥ ħ/2, so ΔE = ħ/(2Δt) = 1.055×10^-34/(2 × 10×10^-9) = 5.28×10^-27 J ≈ 3.3×10^-8 eV. The corresponding line width is Δf = ΔE/h ≈ 7.96×10^6 Hz. For a lifetime of 10^-8 s the width would be about 1.6×10^7 Hz.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Calculate the probability of finding the electron in the ground state of an infinite potential well of length L between x = 0 and x = L/4.
questions.solution: P = ∫0^(L/4) |ψ1|² dx = (2/L) ∫0^(L/4) sin²(πx/L) dx. Using sin²u = (1 - cos2u)/2, P = (2/L)[x/2 - (L/4π)sin(2πx/L)] from 0 to L/4 = 1/4 - 1/(2π) = 0.0908. The probability is therefore about 9.1%.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: An electron is confined in a one-dimensional box of length 0.100 nm. Find the energy values in the lowest three energy states. Find the wavelengths of all photons that can be emitted in downward transitions that eventually carry the electron from n = 3 to n = 1.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Apply the Schrodinger equation to a particle in a one-dimensional box of length L and obtain the energy values of the particle.
questions.solution: Inside the box U = 0, so -(ħ²/2m) d²ψ/dx² = Eψ, giving d²ψ/dx² + k²ψ = 0 with k² = 2mE/ħ². The solution is ψ = A sin kx + B cos kx. The boundary condition ψ(0) = 0 gives B = 0; ψ(L) = 0 gives sin kL = 0, so kL = nπ with n = 1, 2, 3, ... Hence k = nπ/L and E_n = n²π²ħ²/(2mL²) = n²h²/(8mL²). Normalization gives A = sqrt(2/L), so ψ_n = sqrt(2/L) sin(nπx/L).

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: An electron in a one-dimensional box has the wave function ψ(x) = sqrt(2/L) sin(2πx/L). Find (i) its de Broglie wavelength, (ii) its momentum, (iii) its kinetic energy, (iv) the uncertainty in its position and (v) the uncertainty in its momentum.
questions.solution:
Comparing with ψ_n = sqrt(2/L) sin(nπx/L) gives n = 2. (i) λ_dB = 2L/n = L. (ii) p = h/λ = h/L. (iii) KE = p²/2m = h²/(2mL²). (iv) For n = 2, = L/2 and = L²(1/3 - 1/(8π²)), so Δx = L sqrt(1/12 - 1/(8π²)) ≈ 0.266L. (v)

= 0 and = (2πħ/L)², so Δp = 2πħ/L = h/L. The product Δx Δp ≈ 0.266h is consistent with the uncertainty principle.
questions.note: The paper does not state L numerically; the answer is therefore given in terms of the box length L.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Neutrons (mass 1.67 × 10^-27 kg) in thermal equilibrium at room temperature (300 K) have kinetic energy kT, where k is the Boltzmann constant. Find their momentum and de Broglie wavelength.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Calculate the energy of a photon whose frequency is 620 THz. Determine the wavelength of this photon.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: An FM radio transmitter has a power output of 150 kW and operates at 99.7 MHz. How many photons per second does the transmitter emit?

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: A sodium-vapour lamp has a power output of 10.0 W. Using 589.3 nm as the average wavelength, calculate the number of photons emitted per second.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Describe the Davisson-Germer experiment and explain how it proved the wave nature of matter. The interatomic distance in the nickel crystal is 2.15 Å.
questions.solution: Electrons accelerated through a known potential were directed at a nickel crystal and the scattered intensity was measured as a function of angle. A strong maximum appeared at about 50° for 54 V electrons. Using Bragg's law, 2d sinθ = nλ with d = 2.15 Å, the diffracted wavelength was found to be about 1.65 Å. The de Broglie wavelength λ = h/sqrt(2meV) gives 1.67 Å for 54 V. The close agreement confirmed the de Broglie hypothesis and the wave nature of electrons.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Give a brief account of the quantum treatment of a simple harmonic oscillator.
questions.solution: The potential is U = 1/2 kx² = 1/2 mω²x². Solving the Schrodinger equation gives the quantized energies E_v = (v + 1/2)ħω with v = 0, 1, 2, ... The levels are equally spaced by ħω. The lowest state has zero-point energy 1/2 ħω, which the classical oscillator does not have. The wave functions are Hermite polynomials times a Gaussian; the probability density extends into the classically forbidden region, and the correspondence principle is recovered for large v.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: What are the mathematical features of a wave function?
questions.solution: The wave function must be finite, single-valued and continuous everywhere; its first spatial derivative must be finite and continuous; it must be square-integrable so that it can be normalized; and it may be real or complex. These conditions ensure that the probability density is well defined and that the total probability can be set to one.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Sketch schematically the plot of potential energy and its components as a function of internuclear separation for a system of two atoms.
questions.solution: The potential energy is the sum of a long-range attractive term (about -B/r^6) and a short-range repulsive term (about A/r^12). At large r the net energy is small and negative; as r decreases the attractive term dominates and the energy falls to a minimum at the equilibrium separation r0. For r < r0 the repulsive term rises steeply and the energy becomes positive. The depth of the minimum is the dissociation energy of the molecule.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Sketch schematically the radial probability density versus radial distance for the hydrogen atom in the 1s and 2s states.
questions.solution: For 1s, P(r) = (4r²/a0³)e^(-2r/a0), which rises from zero to a single maximum at r = a0 and then decays. For 2s, P(r) has a small inner peak, a node at r = 2a0 where the probability density vanishes, and a larger outer peak around r ≈ 5.2a0. The 2s cloud is therefore larger and has a shell structure.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: If an electron in a hydrogen atom has orbital angular momentum equal to 4.714 × 10^-34 J s, what is the orbital quantum number for the state? What is the lowest principal quantum number in this state? What is the lowest energy of the hydrogen atom in this state?
questions.solution: L = sqrt(l(l+1))ħ. Thus sqrt(l(l+1)) = 4.714×10^-34/1.055×10^-34 = 4.47, so l(l+1) = 20 and l = 4. The lowest principal quantum number is n = l + 1 = 5. The lowest energy is E = -13.6/n² = -13.6/25 = -0.544 eV. The linear momentum of the electron is not a sharp observable; the minimum angular momentum magnitude is the given 4.714×10^-34 J s.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: The potential energy of a diatomic molecule is given by the Lennard-Jones potential U(r) = A/r^12 - B/r^6, where A and B are constants. Find the value of r0 at which the energy is minimum, and the energy E required to break up the molecule. Evaluate r0 and E for H2 with A = 0.124 × 10^-120 eV m^12 and B = 1.488 × 10^-60 eV m^6.
questions.solution: Setting dU/dr = -12A/r^13 + 6B/r^7 = 0 gives r0^6 = 2A/B, so r0 = (2A/B)^(1/6). Substituting A and B: 2A/B = 2 × 0.124×10^-120/1.488×10^-60 = 1.667×10^-60 m^6, so r0 ≈ 1.09×10^-10 m = 0.109 nm. The minimum energy is U(r0) = -B²/(4A) = -(1.488×10^-60)²/(4 × 0.124×10^-120) ≈ -4.46 eV. The energy needed to break the molecule is therefore about 4.46 eV.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Obtain an expression for the quantized rotational energy of a diatomic molecule. From it, obtain expressions for the rotational transition photon energies and frequencies.
questions.solution: A diatomic molecule has moment of inertia I = μr². The rotational energy is E_J = J(J+1)ħ²/2I, J = 0, 1, 2, ... For a transition J → J + 1, ΔE = E_(J+1) - E_J = (J+1)ħ²/I. The emitted or absorbed photon therefore has energy hν = (J+1)ħ²/I and frequency ν = (J+1)ħ/(2πI). The spectrum consists of equally spaced lines.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Give the physical interpretation of the spin magnetic quantum number m_s.
questions.solution: The electron has an intrinsic angular momentum S = sqrt(s(s+1))ħ with s = 1/2. Its projection along a chosen z-axis is S_z = m_s ħ, where m_s = +1/2 (spin up) or -1/2 (spin down). The associated spin magnetic moment is μ_s = -g(e/2m)S with g ≈ 2. The two values correspond to the two possible orientations of the electron spin and explain phenomena such as the fine structure of spectral lines and the Pauli exclusion principle.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: The frequency of the photon that causes the v = 0 to v = 1 transition in the CO molecule is 6.42 × 10^13 Hz. Ignoring changes in rotational energy, calculate (i) the force constant k and (ii) the maximum classical amplitude of vibration for the molecule in the v = 0 state.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: A hydrogen atom is in the first excited state (n = 2). Using the Bohr theory, calculate (i) the radius of the orbit, (ii) the kinetic energy of the electron, (iii) the potential energy of the system and (iv) the total energy.
questions.solution: r_n = 0.529 n² Å, so r_2 = 4 × 0.529 = 2.12 Å. E_n = -13.6/n² eV, so E_2 = -3.4 eV. For a Coulomb-bound electron, KE = -E = +3.4 eV and PE = 2E = -6.8 eV.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Consider the hydrogen atom in the l = 1 state. Calculate the magnitude of the orbital angular momentum, the allowed values of Lz, and the corresponding angles θ that the angular momentum vector makes with the z-axis.
questions.solution: L = sqrt(l(l+1))ħ = sqrt(2)ħ = 1.49×10^-34 J s. For l = 1, m_l = -1, 0, +1, so Lz = -ħ, 0, +ħ. Since cosθ = m_l/sqrt(l(l+1)) = m_l/sqrt2, the angles are θ = 135°, 90° and 45° respectively.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: The J = 0 to J = 1 rotational transition of the CO molecule occurs at a frequency of 1.15 × 10^11 Hz. Calculate the moment of inertia of the molecule and its bond length. What happens if another photon of the same frequency is incident on the CO molecule while it is in the J = 1 state?
questions.solution: For J = 0 → 1, ΔE = ħ²/I = hf, so I = h/(4π²f) = 6.626×10^-34/(4π² × 1.15×10^11) = 1.46×10^-46 kg m². The reduced mass is μ = (12 × 16/28) × 1.66×10^-27 = 1.14×10^-26 kg, so r = sqrt(I/μ) = sqrt(1.46×10^-46/1.14×10^-26) = 1.13×10^-10 m = 0.113 nm. A photon of the same frequency can now drive the J = 1 → 2 transition, since that transition also has energy ħ²/I, so it can be absorbed.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Write mathematical expressions for: (i) potential energy of the H atom, (ii) time-independent 3D Schrodinger equation for the H atom, (iii) electron orbital angular momentum in terms of l, (iv) electron spin angular momentum in terms of s, (v) angle in space quantization in terms of m_l, (vi) magnetic moment of an orbital electron, (vii) Moseley's law, (viii) Boltzmann statistics for populations of states with energies E1 and E2.
questions.solution: (i) U = -e²/(4πε0 r). (ii) -(ħ²/2m)∇²ψ + U(r)ψ = Eψ. (iii) L = sqrt(l(l+1))ħ. (iv) S = sqrt(s(s+1))ħ. (v) cosθ = m_l/sqrt(l(l+1)). (vi) μ = -(e/2m)L. (vii) sqrt(ν) = a(Z - b) for the K series. (viii) N2/N1 = (g2/g1)e^{-(E2 - E1)/kT}.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: A KI molecule contains K+ and I- ions, each with a charge of magnitude e. The ionization energy of K is 4.34 eV and the electron affinity of I is 3.06 eV. What energy is needed to form K+ and I- ions from neutral atoms? What energy is needed to break up a KI molecule into K+ and I- ions? The dissociation energy of KI is 3.37 eV.
questions.solution: Forming K+ requires 4.34 eV and attaching an electron to I releases 3.06 eV, so the net energy to form the ions from neutral atoms is 4.34 - 3.06 = 1.28 eV. Breaking the molecule into ions requires the dissociation energy plus the energy to form the ions: 3.37 + 1.28 = 4.65 eV.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: The wave function for the hydrogen atom in the ground state is ψ(r) = (1/sqrt(π a0³)) e^(-r/a0). Write the expression for the radial probability density and calculate the probability that the electron will be found outside the Bohr radius a0.
questions.solution: The radial probability density is P(r) = 4πr²|ψ|² = (4r²/a0³)e^(-2r/a0). The probability outside a0 is P = ∫_a0^∞ (4r²/a0³)e^(-2r/a0) dr. Substituting x = 2r/a0 gives P = (1/2)∫_2^∞ x²e^(-x)dx = e^-2(1 + 2 + 2) = 5e^-2 ≈ 0.677. Thus about 67.7% of the probability lies outside the Bohr radius.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Taking the effective force constant of a vibrating HCl molecule (masses 1 u and 35 u) as k = 480 N/m, find the energy difference between the ground state and the first excited vibrational level.
questions.solution: The reduced mass is μ = (1 × 35/36) × 1.66×10^-27 = 1.61×10^-27 kg. Angular frequency ω = sqrt(k/μ) = sqrt(480/1.61×10^-27) = 5.45×10^14 rad/s. For a harmonic oscillator, the level spacing is ΔE = ħω = 1.055×10^-34 × 5.45×10^14 = 5.75×10^-20 J ≈ 0.359 eV.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Write an expression for the vibrational energy of a diatomic molecule. Sketch these vibrational energy levels and write an expression for the vibrational transition photon energies.
questions.solution: E_v = (v + 1/2)ħω, v = 0, 1, 2, ..., where ω = sqrt(k/μ). The levels are equally spaced, with a zero-point energy of 1/2 ħω. For the transition v → v + 1, the photon energy is ΔE = ħω and the frequency is ν = ω/2π = (1/2π)sqrt(k/μ).

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: The binding energies of K-shell and L-shell electrons in copper are 8.979 keV and 0.951 keV. A K-alpha X-ray from copper is incident on an NaCl crystal and gives a first-order Bragg reflection at a glancing angle of 15.9° from the alternating planes of sodium atoms. What is the spacing between these planes?
questions.solution: The K-alpha photon energy is 8.979 - 0.951 = 8.028 keV. Its wavelength is λ = hc/E = 1240/8028 = 0.1545 nm. For first-order Bragg reflection, 2d sinθ = λ, so d = 0.1545/(2 sin15.9°) = 0.1545/(2 × 0.2740) = 0.282 nm.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Electrons bombard a molybdenum target, producing continuous and characteristic X-rays. If the accelerating potential is 50.0 kV, find (i) λmin, (ii) λKβ and (iii) λKα. The K, L and M shell energies in molybdenum are -20.0 keV, -2.6 keV and -0.4 keV respectively.
questions.solution: (i) λmin = hc/eV = 1240/50000 = 0.0248 nm = 24.8 pm. (ii) K-beta corresponds to a K → M transition: E = 20.0 - 0.4 = 19.6 keV, so λ = 1240/19600 = 0.0633 nm = 63.3 pm. (iii) K-alpha corresponds to K → L: E = 20.0 - 2.6 = 17.4 keV, so λ = 1240/17400 = 0.0713 nm = 71.3 pm.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Draw a schematic graph of the continuous and characteristic X-ray spectra with labels for the relevant parameters. Obtain an expression for the cutoff wavelength in the continuous X-ray spectrum.
questions.solution: The spectrum has a continuous background that begins at a short-wavelength cutoff λmin and characteristic sharp peaks (K-alpha, K-beta, etc.) superimposed on it. The cutoff arises when an electron loses all its kinetic energy in one collision, producing a photon of maximum energy: eV = hc/λmin, so λmin = hc/eV = 1240/V (nm) with V in volts. Characteristic peaks occur when an electron knocks out an inner-shell electron and another electron fills the vacancy; their wavelengths are fixed by the target's energy levels and follow Moseley's law.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: A 0.00160 nm photon scatters from a free electron. For what photon scattering angle does the recoiling electron have kinetic energy equal to the energy of the scattered photon? The Compton wavelength is 0.00243 nm.
questions.solution: Energy conservation gives hc/λ = hc/λ' + KE. Setting KE = hc/λ' gives hc/λ = 2hc/λ', so λ' = 2λ = 0.00320 nm. The Compton shift is Δλ = 0.00160 nm = 1.60 pm. Using Δλ = λc(1 - cosθ) with λc = 2.43 pm: 1 - cosθ = 1.60/2.43 = 0.658, so cosθ = 0.342 and θ ≈ 70°.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Derive the Compton shift equation.
questions.solution: Let a photon of wavelength λ scatter through angle θ from a stationary electron. Momentum conservation perpendicular and parallel to the incident direction gives p_e sinφ = (h/λ')sinθ and p_e cosφ = h/λ - (h/λ')cosθ. Energy conservation gives hc/λ + mc² = hc/λ' + sqrt(p_e²c² + m²c⁴). Eliminating p_e and φ and simplifying yields Δλ = λ' - λ = (h/mc)(1 - cosθ). The quantity h/mc = 2.43 pm is the Compton wavelength.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Explain the origin of continuous X-rays.
questions.solution: Continuous X-rays (bremsstrahlung) are produced when fast electrons are decelerated by the Coulomb field of target nuclei. The electron loses a variable amount of energy, which appears as a photon; since the energy loss can take any value up to the full kinetic energy, the emitted wavelengths form a continuous spectrum. The shortest wavelength corresponds to the electron losing all its energy in one collision, λmin = hc/eV.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Explain (i) spontaneous emission and (ii) stimulated emission with reference to lasers.
questions.solution: (i) Spontaneous emission: an excited atom decays to a lower level on its own, emitting a photon of energy hf = E2 - E1 in a random direction with a random phase. (ii) Stimulated emission: an incident photon of energy hf induces an excited atom to emit a second photon with the same frequency, phase, polarization and direction, producing coherent light. Laser action requires stimulated emission to dominate, which needs population inversion.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Explain the principle of a laser.
questions.solution: A laser works by light amplification through stimulated emission. The active medium is pumped so that more atoms occupy the upper laser level than the lower level, producing population inversion. A photon then stimulates an excited atom to emit an identical photon, and the two photons stimulate further emission. An optical resonator with mirrors provides feedback, so the light is amplified over many passes; the partially transmitting mirror outputs a coherent, monochromatic, highly directional beam. The basic processes are absorption, spontaneous emission and stimulated emission.

images.caption: Essential laser components: pumping system, lasing medium and resonant cavity.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Describe the construction and working of a ruby laser.
questions.solution: The active medium is a ruby rod (Al2O3 doped with Cr³⁺) with polished ends, one fully silvered and one partially silvered. A helical xenon flash lamp optically pumps the Cr³⁺ ions to a broad band of upper levels. The ions relax non-radiatively to the metastable level, creating population inversion relative to the ground state. Stimulated emission at 694.3 nm then builds up along the rod, and the beam emerges through the partially reflecting end. Ruby is a three-level laser and operates in pulsed mode.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Obtain an expression for the numerical aperture in terms of the refractive indices of the core and cladding, and hence arrive at the condition for ray propagation in an optical fibre.
questions.solution: For a ray entering from a medium n0 at angle θ0, Snell's law gives n0 sinθ0 = n1 sinθ1. At the core-cladding interface, total internal reflection requires the angle of incidence to exceed the critical angle: sin(90° - θ1) ≥ n2/n1, so cosθ1 ≥ n2/n1. Squaring and using sin²θ1 = 1 - cos²θ1 gives n1² sin²θ1 ≤ n1² - n2². Hence n0 sinθ0 ≤ sqrt(n1² - n2²). The numerical aperture is NA = sqrt(n1² - n2²), and the acceptance angle is θ0 = sin⁻¹(NA/n0). Light propagates by repeated total internal reflection as long as the launch angle satisfies this condition.

images.alt: Acceptance cone and numerical aperture of a step-index fibre.
images.caption: Acceptance cone and numerical aperture of a step-index fibre.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: With the help of a neat diagram, explain how transmission of light takes place in optical fibres.
questions.solution: Light entering the core at an angle within the acceptance cone refracts at the core end and then strikes the core-cladding boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle. It undergoes total internal reflection and travels along the fibre in a zigzag path, losing very little energy. This repeated total internal reflection guides the light over long distances. A core of higher refractive index surrounded by a cladding of lower refractive index is essential.

images.alt: Acceptance cone and numerical aperture of a step-index fibre.
images.caption: Acceptance cone and numerical aperture of a step-index fibre.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Define an energy band. Sketch the energy bands of a sodium crystal containing N atoms, label each band and indicate the number of allowed energy states in each band.
questions.solution: An energy band is a range of closely spaced allowed electron energies formed when atomic energy levels split and overlap in a solid. Sodium has the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹. In a crystal of N atoms, the 1s, 2s and 2p bands are full and lie well below the Fermi level. The 3s band holds 2N states and is half filled (N electrons); it overlaps the empty 3p band, which is why sodium is a conductor. Each band contains 2N states per atomic level when spin is included.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: The band gap energy for silicon at 300 K is 1.14 eV. Find the lowest-frequency photon that will promote an electron from the valence band to the conduction band.
questions.solution: The photon energy must equal the band gap: hf = Eg. Thus f = Eg/h = 1.14 × 1.6×10^-19/6.626×10^-34 = 2.75×10^14 Hz, corresponding to λ = c/f = 1.09×10^-6 m = 1090 nm.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Consider a cube of gold 1.00 mm on an edge. Calculate the approximate number of conduction electrons whose energies lie between 4.000 eV and 4.025 eV. The density of states is g(E) = (8π√2 m^(3/2)/h³)√E per unit volume per unit energy.
questions.solution: The coefficient 8π√2 m^(3/2)/h³ = 1.06×10^56 (SI). At E = 4.00 eV = 6.41×10^-19 J, sqrt(E) = 8.01×10^-10, so g(E) = 8.50×10^46 states per m³ per J. The energy interval is 0.025 eV = 4.01×10^-21 J and the volume is (10^-3)³ = 10^-9 m³. Hence N = g(E) ΔE V = 8.50×10^46 × 4.01×10^-21 × 10^-9 ≈ 3.4×10^17 electrons.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Assuming the expression for the allowed states of a particle in a three-dimensional box, derive the density-of-states function.
questions.solution: For a box of volume V, the allowed wave vectors are spaced by 2π/L in each direction, so the number of states in a shell between k and k + dk is (V/2π³)4πk²dk, with a factor 2 for spin. For a free electron E = ħ²k²/2m, so k = sqrt(2mE)/ħ and dk = m dE/(ħ²k). Substituting gives g(E)dE = (V/2π²)(2m/ħ²)^(3/2) sqrt(E) dE. Thus g(E) = (8π√2 m^(3/2)/h³)V sqrt(E), which increases as the square root of energy.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Calculate the energy of a conduction electron in silver at 800 K, assuming the probability of finding an electron in that state is 0.950. The Fermi energy is 5.48 eV at this temperature.
questions.solution: The Fermi-Dirac function is f(E) = 1/[e^((E - EF)/kT) + 1]. Rearranging, E = EF + kT ln(1/f - 1). Here kT = 8.617×10^-5 × 800 = 0.0689 eV and ln(1/0.95 - 1) = ln(0.0526) = -2.944. Hence E = 5.48 - 0.203 = 5.28 eV.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Explain a light emitting diode with a band diagram.
questions.solution: An LED is a forward-biased p-n junction made from a direct-bandgap semiconductor. Electrons injected into the p-side recombine with holes near the junction, releasing energy as photons with hf ≈ Eg. The band diagram shows the conduction band above the valence band with the depletion region reduced under forward bias. The emission wavelength is λ ≈ 1240/Eg (nm, with Eg in eV), so the band gap determines the colour.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Explain the classification of solids regarding their electrical properties, based on their energy band diagrams.
questions.solution: Conductors have a partially filled band or overlapping bands, so electrons can move freely with no band gap. Semiconductors have a small band gap (about 1 eV) and a filled valence band at 0 K; at ordinary temperatures thermal excitation promotes some electrons to the conduction band, giving a modest conductivity that increases with temperature. Insulators have a large band gap (several eV), so essentially no electrons reach the conduction band and conductivity is negligible. The band gap and the position of the Fermi level therefore determine the electrical behaviour.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Write the expression for the Fermi-Dirac distribution function and sketch its plots for zero K and for T > 0 K.
questions.solution: f(E) = 1/[e^((E - EF)/kT) + 1]. At T = 0 K the function is a step: f = 1 for E < EF and f = 0 for E > EF, with a sharp drop at EF. For T > 0 K the step broadens over an energy range of order kT around EF: f = 1/2 at E = EF, and the curve tails into the conduction band and below the Fermi level.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Sodium is a monovalent metal with density 971 kg/m³ and molar mass 0.023 kg/mol. Calculate (i) the density of charge carriers and (ii) the Fermi energy at zero K. Use EF = (ħ²/2m)(3π²n)^(2/3) and Avogadro's number 6.023 × 10^23 /mol.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Show that the average kinetic energy of a conduction electron in a metal at zero K is (3/5)EF, using the density of conduction electrons n = (8π/3h³)(2mEF)^(3/2) and the density of states.
questions.solution: At T = 0 all states up to EF are filled. The average energy is <E> = (1/n)∫0^EF E g(E) dE with g(E) = C sqrt(E). Thus the integral is C ∫0^EF E^(3/2)dE = (2/5)C EF^(5/2). The electron density is n = ∫0^EF C sqrt(E)dE = (2/3)C EF^(3/2). Dividing gives <E> = [(2/5)/(2/3)]EF = (3/5)EF.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Light from a hydrogen discharge tube is incident on a CdS crystal with band gap 2.42 eV. Which spectral lines from the Balmer series (656 nm, 486 nm, 434 nm, 410 nm) are absorbed and which are transmitted?
questions.solution: The threshold wavelength is λ = 1240/Eg = 1240/2.42 = 512 nm. Photons with wavelengths shorter than 512 nm have enough energy to excite electrons across the gap and are absorbed. Thus 486 nm, 434 nm and 410 nm are absorbed, while 656 nm (energy below the gap) is transmitted.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Derive an expression for the density of conduction electrons in an intrinsic semiconductor. Given the energy density of states g(E) = (2^(7/2)π m_c^(3/2)/h³)(E - E_c)^(1/2), where m_c is the conduction electron mass and E_c is the conduction band edge.
questions.solution: n = ∫_(E_c)^∞ g(E) f(E) dE. For an intrinsic semiconductor the Fermi level lies well below E_c, so f(E) ≈ e^{-(E - EF)/kT}. Let x = E - E_c. Then n = (2^(7/2)π m_c^(3/2)/h³) e^{-(E_c - EF)/kT} ∫0^∞ sqrt(x) e^{-x/kT} dx. The integral is (sqrt(π)/2)(kT)^(3/2). Simplifying gives n = 2(2π m_c kT/h²)^(3/2) e^{-(E_c - EF)/kT}. Multiplying by the analogous expression for holes and using np = n_i² gives n_i = 2(2πkT/h²)^(3/2)(m_c m_v)^(3/4) e^{-Eg/2kT}.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Draw the energy band diagrams of (i) an n-type semiconductor, (ii) a p-type semiconductor and (iii) an unbiased p-n junction. Indicate the positions of the relevant energy levels and the Fermi level at 0 K.
questions.solution: (i) n-type: donor levels lie just below the conduction band; the Fermi level is close to the conduction band. (ii) p-type: acceptor levels lie just above the valence band; the Fermi level is close to the valence band. (iii) Unbiased p-n junction: the bands bend across the depletion region, creating a potential barrier; the Fermi level is constant across the junction at equilibrium, and the depletion region has no free carriers.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: The Hall coefficient of a p-type semiconductor is 1.00 × 10^-4 m³/C and its conductivity is 500.0 S/m. Calculate the resistivity, the number of holes per unit volume and the mobility of the holes.

questions.question: Find the conductivity of silicon at 300 K (i) in the intrinsic condition, (ii) with a donor impurity of 1 in 10^8 and (iii) with an acceptor impurity of 1 in 5 × 10^7. The intrinsic carrier density is 1.5 × 10^16 m^-3, electron mobility 0.13 m²/V s, hole mobility 0.05 m²/V s and the density of silicon atoms is 5 × 10^28 m^-3.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Most solar radiation has a wavelength of about 1 μm. What energy gap should the material in a solar cell have in order to absorb this radiation?
questions.solution: Eg = hc/λ = 1.988×10^-25/1.0×10^-6 = 1.99×10^-19 J ≈ 1.24 eV. A band gap of about 1.2 eV is therefore needed.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Give a brief account of superconductivity.
questions.solution: Below a critical temperature Tc, certain materials lose all electrical resistance and become superconductors. They also expel magnetic flux (Meissner effect) and behave as perfect diamagnets. The transition is accompanied by a jump in specific heat and is explained by BCS theory: electrons pair through lattice vibrations into Cooper pairs, which condense into a ground state with an energy gap. Superconductors are destroyed by a sufficiently strong magnetic field (critical field) or by a large current density.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Explain the Meissner effect in superconductors.
questions.solution: When a material becomes superconducting, it expels the magnetic field from its interior, so B = 0 inside. This perfect diamagnetism (magnetic susceptibility χ = -1) is the Meissner effect. It is not merely a consequence of zero resistance: the field is actively expelled during the transition, and a sufficiently strong applied field can destroy the superconducting state.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Determine the current generated in a superconducting ring of niobium metal 2.00 cm in diameter when a 0.0200 T magnetic field directed perpendicular to the ring is suddenly decreased to zero. The inductance of the ring is 3.10 × 10^-8 H.
questions.solution: The flux through the ring is Φ = BA = 0.0200 × π(0.0100)² = 6.28×10^-6 Wb. A superconducting ring conserves flux, so the induced current satisfies LI = Φ. Thus I = 6.28×10^-6/3.10×10^-8 ≈ 203 A.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Draw a representative graph of resistance versus temperature for a superconductor and explain briefly the BCS theory of superconductivity in metals.
questions.solution: The resistance falls gradually with temperature and then drops abruptly to zero at Tc. In BCS theory, an electron moving through the lattice attracts positive ions, creating a temporary region of positive charge that attracts a second electron. The resulting electron-phonon interaction binds electrons of opposite momentum and spin into Cooper pairs. These pairs behave as bosons, condense into a single quantum ground state and move without scattering, giving zero resistance below Tc. Breaking a pair requires energy 2Δ, which produces the observed energy gap.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Explain (i) Stefan's law, (ii) Wien's displacement law and (iii) the Rayleigh-Jeans law.
questions.solution: (i) Stefan's law: the total energy radiated per unit area per unit time by a blackbody is proportional to T⁴, P/A = σT⁴. (ii) Wien's displacement law: the wavelength of maximum emission is inversely proportional to temperature, λmT = 2.898×10^-3 m K. (iii) Rayleigh-Jeans law: the spectral radiance of a blackbody is I(λ,T) = 2πckBT/λ⁴, which agrees with experiment at long wavelengths but diverges as λ → 0, leading to the ultraviolet catastrophe.

questions.subject: engineering-physics
questions.question: Find the peak wavelength of the blackbody radiation emitted by the tungsten filament of a light bulb operating at 2000 K. Sketch the intensity versus wavelength graph.
questions.solution: By Wien's law, λm = 2.898×10^-3/T = 2.898×10^-3/2000 = 1.45×10^-6 m = 1450 nm. The peak lies in the infrared, which is why an incandescent bulb emits relatively little visible light. The intensity-wavelength curve rises to a maximum at 1450 nm and then falls off at shorter wavelengths.
